newsitem.title: GERMANY: DASA ups stakes in Airbus-Boeing struggle.
newsitem.headline: DASA ups stakes in Airbus-Boeing struggle.

text.p: Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) has upped the stakes in the battle for the big passenger jet market by suggesting newly-merged Boeing-McDonnell Douglas had leant on a potential U.S. Airbus supplier, analysts said.

DASA chairman Manfred Bischoff said on Thursday that Boeing had indicated to a U.S. supplier -- which DASA confirmed was Northrop Grumman -- it would be "an unfriendly act" to join the planned Airbus A3XX super-large aircraft project.
Although Bischoff's remarks stopped short of accusing Boeing of anti-competitive behaviour, he warned competition in the aircraft industry could harden along transatlantic lines.
"It would be unwise to move the line of competition to the Atlantic," Bischoff told reporters.
DASA -- a unit of auto giant Daimler-Benz AG -- is a partner with France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace and Spain's CASA in the European Airbus consortium.
A spokesman at Airbus' French headquarters said on Friday there had been no evidence of any kind of pressure. But an industry source close to the consortium said: "It is a fact."
Aircraft industry analysts interpreted Bischoff's comments more as an effort to boost the A3XX project than an attack on the new Boeing's market dominance.

"It's the rationale behind the comments, not the comments themselves," said Charles Armitage, analyst at Lehman Brothers in London. "Both sides are posturing, and it's in their interest to make life as difficult as possible for Boeing."
DASA is a keen backer of the A3XX -- a 555-seat aircraft which it says would cost $10 billion to build and could fly by 2003. Both industry analysts and Boeing say it would cost more.

Boeing itself has dropped plans for a stretch version of its trusty 747 Jumbo jet, saying the potential market was too small. But Airbus managing director Jean Pierson said on Thursday in France that Boeing could launch a new model later "to cut the ground from under Airbus".

Airbus is seeking partners to take a 40 percent share in the A3XX and has managed to get Italy's Alenia on board. Saab of Sweden is interested, as are South Korean firms. Aerospatiale has also courted U.S. Lockheed Martin.
But analyst Nick Cunningham of BZW in London said pressing ahead with developing the A3XX would be a "significant mistake" as the plane would be ready before the market has matured.
Cunningham also doubted that Boeing was seriously trying to spoil the A3XX project. "To be honest, why would Boeing bother if it is not competing directly?" he said.

Analysts said Airbus would do much better to focus on developing new models of the A340 range to compete directly with some of the aging early series Boeing 747s. The A340-600 could carry 375 passengers, while the long-range A340-500 would be able to fly non-stop from Dallas to Hong Kong.
Bischoff said on Thursday he was keen to see both the A3XX and the new A340s realised, although financing their development simultaneously would not be possible.
"Developments will not and cannot take place at the same time due to technical and financial questions," Bischoff told reporters. "But we will do all possible to realise both."

No immediate response to Bischoff's comments was available from the office of European Union competition commissioner Karel Van Miert, who said in January he would examine the implications of the Boeing merger.
